extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of hydrostatics / hydraulics (readers of a physics treatise)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, experimental demonstrations, and practical guidance about fluid pressure (vertical, lateral, and oblique) in single and multiple immiscible fluids, and their application to hydraulic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Altitude / Pressure depends on height not breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure (upwards and downwards) that fluids exert on parts of a horizontal plane adapts to the Height (or Depth) of the fluid above that part and by no means to their Breadth or Surface. ('...it adapts itself only to the Height (or Depth) of Fluids, but by no means to their Breadth or Surface.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown repeatedly by experiments with tubes and vessels: moving or changing breadth while holding the same vertical heights leaves the pressure unchanged. Practical implication: when analysing water-works, represent the pressure on a part by the column of fluid above it regardless of vessel width.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of pressure on equal parts of the same horizontal plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more equal parts of a horizontal plane in a fluid (or in stacked fluids) are each pressed upwards and downwards with the weight of their columns of altitude, and thus with equal force. ('Two or more equal Parts thereof... will each of 'em be press'd up-wards and downwards, with the Weight of their Columns of Altitude, and consequently with equal Force.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when parts communicate within the same fluid (i.e., a path exists in the same fluid between them). This underlies many constructions using communicating vessels and equal-height arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-part pressure equals weight of the perpendicular column of fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: The force pressing each (small) part upon another equals the weight of the perpendicular column of the fluid whose base is that part and whose top reaches to the upper surface of the highest incumbent fluid. ('That the Force which presseth each Part upon the other, is equal to the Weight of the perpendicular Column of the Fluid.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operative statement used to compute pressures: replace the actual (possibly broad) vessel by an equivalent perpendicular column of the same cross-section and height to find the pressure on the base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column of Altitude for multiple immiscible fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: When several immiscible fluids are incumbent upon each other, the column of altitude consists of the stacked heights of each fluid above the point; each stacked height presses with its own particular weight, and the total pressure is the sum of these contributions. ('...the Column of Altitude consists of a Pillar... composed of the several Depths of the Pickle BW, of the Oil WX, and of the Air XZ... each Height... presses downwards with the particular Weight of every Fluid of which it is the Height.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute pressure at a point beneath layered fluids, sum the weights (specific gravities) times respective layer heights; experiments with quicksilver and tubes illustrate and validate this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward pressure proceeds only from lateral fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: A part of a horizontal plane is never pressed upwards by the fluid directly beneath it alone but only by lateral parts of fluids that are higher; thus upward pressure arises from adjacent (lateral) fluid rather than vertical columns directly under the part. ('...that they are never press'd upwards, but by Fluids that are not only higher, but also lateral; and other Parts of the same Horizontal Plane press downwards: So that all Pressure upwards proceeds from these Lateral Fluids...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains behaviour in tubes and communicating vessels: removing lateral fluid causes the suspended columns within tubes to fall. Use lateral-fluid reasoning when considering support of local elevations in fluid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique (curved) columns exert same pressure as equivalent perpendicular column
rubrics_metrics.description: An oblique or curved column of fluid that rests upon a horizontal part exerts neither more nor less pressure than a straight perpendicular column having the same base and the same perpendicular height to the upper surface. ('...the Preſsure it undergoes is neither greater nor less, than that of the Column of Altitude; that is, of the Perpendicular Column...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence fountain jets or curved ducts do not change the pressure on the pressed part provided the perpendicular height to the free surface is the same. The shape or quantity (width) of the oblique tube does not affect the local pressure if the perpendicular height is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lateral pressure adapts to vertical height, not to fluid quantity/breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The lateral (sideways) pressure a fluid exerts on a vertical surface depends on the vertical height of fluid above each point of the surface and not on the total breadth or amount of the fluid. ('...the Lateral Pressure does by no means adapt itself to the Breadth or Quantity of the Water...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by streams from side holes and by placing partitions that change breadth without altering height: the horizontal range/force changes only with height. For calculating lateral force on a plane, divide plane into small elements each bearing lateral pressure equal to weight of column above that element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic law of lateral pressures (integral/half-rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total lateral pressure on a vertical plane AE (made up of many small elements) equals the sum of contributions from the heights above each element; in the discrete example given the lateral pressure on AE equals half of the total weight that the equal-area horizontal plane EI would bear under the same top-to-bottom heights (i.e., proportional to the mean height). ('...the lateral Pressure upon AE... is the half of ... the Preſsure downwards, which the said AE if it lay horizontally at EI... would suffer...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an integrated statement: when discretizing the vertical surface into many small horizontal strips, the lateral force equals the integral of pressure (= density * g * height) over the area; experimental balances and measurements (wooden plate burst tests) validate the computed value. Use fine subdivision (elements → points) to reduce discretization error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local equality of lateral and perpendicular pressures for sufficiently small parts
rubrics_metrics.description: For sufficiently small parts/elements, the lateral (sideways) pressure exerted by a fluid on a vertical element is essentially equal to the perpendicular (downward) pressure exerted on a horizontal element having the same small area and the same fluid height above it. (Experimental bottle/tube demonstration in air and in water.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical experiments: small or infinitesimal elements can be compared directly (use small tubes/holes and careful sealing). The result justifies replacing small planar elements with equivalent horizontal elements when computing local pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental methods and precautions for measuring pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of communicating tubes, quicksilver (mercury) manometers, sealed bottles with tubes, balances and wooden plates to measure and compare vertical, lateral and oblique pressures; take care with tube diameters and wetting (liquid sticking to sides) to avoid artefacts. ('...take care you do not pour them in at first to the Height required; because the Tube not being very large, when that which sticks to the Sides at pouring in comes to subside, it will cause it to rise higher than in the Vessel. This may be obviated perhaps by first filling the Tube...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow described experimental setups to verify laws (curve tube figures, quicksilver columns). Seal joints to prevent air leaks; place measurement points at same horizontal plane; be aware of capillary/wetting effects in narrow tubes; compare results in air and in other fluids to isolate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to hydraulic works: represent pressure by an equivalent column
rubrics_metrics.description: To inquire into the nature of any water-works with respect to water pressure, single out a small horizontal part and represent the pressure upon it by a Column of Altitude ABZ whose base is that part and whose height reaches to the upper surface of the highest fluid; pressure on the part equals weight of that equivalent column. ('So that to know with what Weight 4b, in the Vessel, is prest; it may be answer'd, with the Column of Altitude ABZ...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This representation simplifies engineering calculations for fountains, pumps, and vessels: one can imagine extending the horizontal plane outward and setting an equal column to compute the load. Use layered columns for multiple fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: General hydrostatical proposition (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: If several fluids are incumbent upon each other and a horizontal plane passes through one of them, equal parts of that plane will be pressed upward and downward with the weight of their columns of altitude; thus one part is pressed downwards with the same force as another part is pressed upwards, and vice versa (concise statement of the hydrostatic laws previously derived).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as the central axiom for the other derived rules (oblique, lateral, layered fluids). Use this proposition to deduce consequences for communicating vessels, fountain designs, and force balances in hydraulic devices.
